original_question: For the Rado graph, does the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings have the same reverse-mathematical strength as the rainbow Ramsey property for (k + 1)-bounded colorings?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem (10), referring back to statement (D): "Does the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings of the Rado graph have the same reverse math strength as for (k + 1)-bounded colorings?"
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact topic, structure, and comparison in the paper: it is about the Rado graph, the rainbow Ramsey property, k-bounded versus (k+1)-bounded colorings, and equality of reverse-mathematical strength. It is very close to the paper's official wording in Section 2, Problem (10).
missing_details: The paper's problem is posed in the reverse-mathematical setting, so to make it stand-alone it should be stated as an equivalence question over the usual base theory RCA0.
The parameter k should be treated as a fixed integer with k >= 2, matching the formulation of the rainbow Ramsey property given in Section 1.

The phrase "rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings of the Rado graph" should be unpacked: for every finite graph G, every coloring of all copies of G in the Rado graph R into countably many colors such that each color is used at most k times, there is a subgraph R' of R that is again a Rado graph and in which no two copies of G receive the same color.
The problem is not restricted to edge colorings; in the paper, statement (D) quantifies over arbitrary finite graphs G.
The comparison is specifically between the k-bounded and (k+1)-bounded versions of statement (D), not a broader comparison with other rainbow Ramsey principles.
refined_question: For a fixed integer k >= 2, over RCA0, is the following k-bounded rainbow Ramsey principle for the Rado graph equivalent to its (k+1)-bounded version: for every finite graph G, every coloring of all copies of G in the Rado graph R into countably many colors with each color used at most k times admits a subgraph R' subseteq R that is again a Rado graph and in which no two copies of G have the same color?
justification: The draft is already aimed at the exact official problem in the paper: Section 2, Problem (10). The paper does not formulate this as a theorem or conjecture elsewhere; instead, it first defines in Section 1 what the rainbow Ramsey property for the Rado graph means, packages that as statement (D), and then asks in Problem (10) whether the k-bounded and (k+1)-bounded versions have the same reverse-mathematical strength. The refinement therefore stays narrow and paper-faithful by only adding the hidden content of statement (D), the parameter restriction k >= 2, and the ambient reverse-mathematical base theory RCA0 that is part of the surrounding setup.
